intro: Millions of people around the world use healing traditions that are hundreds or thousands of years old. A grandmother in Chicago brews an herbal tea. A doctor in Beijing offers acupuncture after surgery. A family in Tokyo picks up a packet of Kampo herbs from the pharmacy. These traditions carry culture, family memory and real knowledge.

This unit looks at Traditional Chinese Medicine, Ayurveda, Unani, Kampo and healing traditions of the Americas. First you will learn each tradition's ideas in its own terms. Then you will ask the questions scientists ask: What was tested? Compared with what? What did the results show? Some practices, such as tai chi for balance and yoga for back pain, have held up in careful tests. One old recipe led to a Nobel Prize.

By the end, you will be able to explain a tradition respectfully, read a study's result carefully, and name the risks of herbs and supplements. You will also know the single most useful habit for safe care: telling your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about everything you take.
bigQuestion: How can we honor traditional medicine and still let evidence decide what helps?

timeline.t: The Yellow Emperor's Inner Classic, a founding TCM text, takes shape in China
Classic Ayurvedic texts are compiled in India
Ge Hong writes a handbook of emergency remedies, including qinghao for fevers
Ibn Sina completes the Canon of Medicine, a foundation of Unani medicine
Japan's national health insurance begins covering many Kampo formulas
Tu Youyou's team finds a sweet wormwood extract that clears malaria in animals
The U.S. creates a National Institutes of Health center to study complementary medicine
A JAMA study finds heavy metals in about one in five Ayurvedic products bought online
India creates the Ministry of AYUSH for traditional systems of medicine
Tu Youyou shares the Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine for artemisinin
The American College of Physicians advises non-drug options like yoga for chronic low back pain

words.d: in TCM, the vital energy believed to flow through the body
in TCM, the channels through which qi is said to flow
in Chinese thought, two opposite but linked qualities that must stay in balance
a fake treatment made to look like the real one, used for comparison in a study
real improvement that comes from expecting to get better and from care, not the treatment itself
a malaria drug first isolated from sweet wormwood by Tu Youyou's team
a change in how a medicine works because of an herb taken at the same time
in Ayurveda, the three forces, vata, pitta and kapha, said to shape body and mind
metals such as lead, mercury and arsenic that can harm the body
a tradition based on Greek medicine as developed by Arabic and Persian physicians
Japanese herbal medicine adapted from Chinese medicine
care that combines standard medicine with complementary practices that have evidence for a use

test.q: In Traditional Chinese Medicine, what is qi?
choices: The vital energy said to flow through the body
test.why: TCM teaches that qi is vital energy flowing through the meridians.

test.q: What do many sham-controlled acupuncture trials show?
choices: Real and sham acupuncture often give similar results
No one feels better in either group
test.why: Many sham-controlled trials find similar results for real and sham acupuncture.

test.q: Which practice has good evidence for preventing falls in older adults?
test.why: Trials show tai chi improves balance and lowers falls in older adults.

test.q: What clue did Tu Youyou find in Ge Hong's handbook?
choices: Soak the herb in water rather than heating it
test.why: Ge Hong described soaking qinghao in water, which suggested heat destroyed the active chemical.

test.q: What is an ACT used to treat?
test.why: An artemisinin-based combination therapy is a main treatment for malaria.

test.q: Which risk is linked to some herbal products?
choices: Contamination with heavy metals or hidden drugs
test.why: Tests have found heavy metals, hidden drugs or the wrong plant in some herbal products.

test.q: Why do many TCM groups support substitutes for rhino horn and tiger bone?
choices: The animals are endangered and there is no good evidence the products work
test.why: These animals are endangered, and there is no good scientific evidence that rhino horn treats disease.

test.q: Which of these is one of Ayurveda's three doshas?
test.why: Ayurveda's doshas are vata, pitta and kapha.

test.q: What is the difference between recognition and proof?
choices: Recognition shows a society values a tradition; proof comes from fair trials
test.why: Government recognition is not the same as scientific proof, which requires fair tests.

test.q: What does the evidence show about turmeric's curcumin?
choices: Promising in the lab, limited proof in people
test.why: Curcumin looks promising in preclinical studies but has limited proof in people.

test.q: Which tradition kept the Greek idea of the four humors?
test.why: Unani medicine grew from Greek medicine and still uses the four humors as its framework.

test.q: How is Kampo usually prescribed in Japan?
choices: By medical doctors within the national health system
test.why: In Japan, medical doctors prescribe many Kampo formulas covered by national insurance.

choices: Using unproven remedies instead of standard care
Adding evidence-based complementary practices to standard care
test.why: Integrative medicine combines standard care with complementary practices that have evidence.

test.q: Which Chicago example appears in this unit?
choices: A botanica in Pilsen selling herbs
An Ayurvedic college in the Loop
A TCM hospital run by the city
test.why: The unit describes a botanica in Chicago's Pilsen neighborhood.

test.q: What is the most useful habit for safe care with herbs and supplements?
choices: Telling your doctor, nurse or pharmacist about everything you take
test.why: The unit stresses telling your clinicians about every herb and supplement so they can check for interactions.

write.prompt: Should hospitals in the United States offer traditional practices such as acupuncture, tai chi or yoga? Take a position. Use two or three facts or sources from this unit, and explain how the evidence supports your claim.
tips: Name the practice and the specific use you are arguing about.
Cite at least two facts or sources from the unit, such as a trial result or a guideline.
Describe the tradition respectfully and state the other side fairly.
Use unit terms like sham, placebo effect and integrative medicine.
End with a clear claim and one safety point.
